name: Timor-Leste
summary_text: Timor-Leste does not criminalise same-sex sexual conduct. Same-sex sexual acts have been legal since 1975, and no source records anti-trans legislation, arrest patterns, or police targeting of trans people in the country. No law restricting trans people from public facilities, health care, or employment is documented.  No legal gender recognition procedure exists in Timor-Leste. For a visitor, the operative document is therefore the passport or identity card issued in the home jurisdiction, including any gender marker changed there. There is no domestic route by which a foreign trans person could alter or regularise a marker while in the country.  Official signals run in a supportive direction at the highest level. The Prime Minister gave televised endorsement to the country's first Pride parade in 2017, and President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the 2019 march, stating that he is a president for all people. Day-to-day rejection is nonetheless documented alongside those statements, including hostile messages sent to the family of a Pride organiser, so public visibility attracts both state endorsement and social hostility.  Pride marches are held annually in Dili, in July. A visitor present during those weeks can expect a visible public event of a scale that has grown substantially since 2017.

sources.title: Law on Domestic Violence No. 07/2010
sources.documents: Expands definition of family to include people who live or have lived in conditions analogous to spouses, broadly encompassing intimate relationships regardless of gender.
sources.detail: Cited as 'Law on Domestic Violence No. 07/2010'. No URL visible in text.

sources.title: 2017 United States Department of State Human Rights Report on Timor-Leste
sources.documents: Documents status of LGBTQ rights: constitution/law silent on same-sex relations; PDHJ work with CODIVA; verbal abuse and discrimination in public services including medical centers; particular vulnerability of transgender persons; corrective rape, abuse, ostracism; education and employment discrimination; 2017 Pride March and PM support.
sources.detail: Cited as '2017 United States Department of State report' under 'Human rights reports' with quoted sections on Acts of Violence, Discrimination, and Other Abuses Based on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Discrimination with Respect to Employment and Occupation. No URL visible.

sources.title: Penal Code aggravating circumstance (since 2009) and Law No. 3/2017 on Prevention and Fight against Human Trafficking and Fourth Amendment to Penal Code, Article 3
sources.documents: Establishes bias on basis of sexual orientation as aggravating circumstance for crimes; requires victim protection measures without discrimination based on sexual orientation.
sources.detail: Cited as 'Since 2009, bias on the basis of sexual orientation has been considered to be an aggravating circumstance' and 'Law No. 3/2017... Article 3'. No URL visible.

sources.title: Timor-Leste Constitution drafting history (2002) - rejected sexual orientation non-discrimination clause
sources.documents: Documents lack of broad constitutional protection: original draft clause against discrimination based on sexual orientation voted out by 52 out of 88 MPs before Constitution took effect in 2002; opposition influenced by Catholic Church.
sources.detail: Cited as clause 'included in the original draft of the Timorese Constitution but it was voted out by 52 out of 88 MPs'. No URL visible.

sources.title: 2017 Bella Galhos survey / November Rede Feto study of lesbian, bisexual women and transgender men in Dili and Bobonaro
sources.documents: Documents documented incidents: 86% of 57 respondents experienced physical and psychological violence including domestic violence, forced marriages, attempts to change sexual orientation/gender identity; corrective rape, ostracism, marginalization; removal from home, school bullying/dropout for transgender students.
sources.detail: Cited as '2017 survey of 57 young lesbian and bisexual women as well as transgender men co-authored by activist Bella Galhos' and 'November study conducted for Rede Feto'. No URL visible.

sources.title: National Police statutes: Decree-Law No. 44/2020 Article 13(1); Decree-Law No. 69/2022 Articles 15(6)(f), 18(b); Decree-Law No. 35/2024 Articles 16-17
sources.documents: Rights machinery for enforcement: police duty to treat people with respect without discrimination based on sexual orientation; bans discrimination; requires missions be carried out without hindrance by sexual orientation.
sources.detail: Cited with decree numbers and article numbers under 'National Police'. No URL visible.

sources.title: Law No. 6/2023 on Protection of Children and Young People in Danger Article 6(n) and Ministerial Decree No. 11/MSSI/V/2024 SOP
sources.documents: Establishes broad protections for LGBTI children/youth: equal rights without discrimination based on sex, gender, sexual orientation; defines gender, non-binary gender identity, LGBTI children, sexual and gender-based violence; requires non-discriminatory case management and care for transgender children at risk of prejudice, stigma, violence.
sources.detail: Cited as 'Law No. 6/2023... Article 6(n)' and 'Ministerial Decree No. 11/MSSI/V/2024 approving Standard Operating Procedures'. No URL visible.

sources.title: Health protections: Law No. 13/2022 Article 3-2(o) amending Health System Law and Decree-Law No. 88/2022 Article 3-B(e); 2019 Minister inquiry call
sources.documents: Requires health policy and health professionals to provide care without discrimination based on gender identity and sexual orientation; 2019 Minister of Legislative Reform call to end LGBTQ discrimination and request official inquiry into alleged ill-treatment of disabled and LGBTQ patients at national hospital in Dili.
sources.detail: Cited as 'Law No. 13/2022, Second amendment to Law No. 10/2004' and 'Decree-Law No. 88/2022' plus April 2019 minister statement in National Parliament. No URL visible.
